p: Richard Cromwell, Lord Protector from 1658 to 1659, ceded power to the Rump Parliament, and for a year government was dominated by the army leaders Charles Fleetwood and John Lambert. On 20 October 1659 George Monck, governor of Scotland under the Cromwells, marched south to oppose them. Lambert's army melted away and Monck reached London unopposed. The Presbyterian members excluded in Pride's Purge of 1648 were recalled, and on 24 December the Long Parliament was restored.

On 4 April 1660 Charles issued the Declaration of Breda, setting out his promises on recovering the crown. Monck organised the Convention Parliament, which first met on 25 April and on 8 May proclaimed that Charles II had been lawful king since the execution of Charles I on 30 January 1649. Charles left The Hague on 23 May, landed at Dover on 25 May and entered London on 29 May, his thirtieth birthday, a date kept afterwards as the holiday of Oak Apple Day. He was crowned at Westminster Abbey on 23 April 1661.

The Indemnity and Oblivion Act, law from 29 August 1660, pardoned past treason but excluded those involved in the trial and execution of Charles I. In October 1660 ten men were hanged, drawn and quartered in London, among them Thomas Harrison and the preacher Hugh Peters; three more followed on 19 April 1662, and a further 19 were imprisoned for life. In January 1661 the corpses of Oliver Cromwell, Henry Ireton and John Bradshaw were exhumed and hanged in chains at Tyburn.

The Cavalier Parliament, overwhelmingly royalist, met on 8 May 1661 and sat until 24 January 1679. The leading minister of the first years was Edward Hyde, 1st Earl of Clarendon, and the Church of England was restored as the national church, backed by the Clarendon Code and the Act of Uniformity 1662. In Scotland the Rescissory Act 1661 annulled all legislation back to 1633; in Ireland the union of the Commonwealth years was treated as void, and James Butler, 1st Duke of Ormond, returned as Lord Lieutenant in 1662.

The colonies followed at different speeds. Barbados declared for the king in July 1660, Rhode Island in October 1660 and Massachusetts last, in August 1661; New Haven, which sheltered three regicides, was merged into Connecticut in 1662. The period is commonly taken to end with the Glorious Revolution of 1688, when William of Orange landed on 5 November and James II fled to France, and with the Bill of Rights 1689.

notes: The article says twelve regicides were condemned and ten executed in October 1660, 'at Charing Cross or Tyburn'; I gave the ten and 'in London'.
The article says Lambert 'died in custody in 1684' and elsewhere that he stayed in custody in Guernsey for life; left out.
Oak Apple Day: the article says 29 May was made a holiday to celebrate his return and, under Ireland, that this was done in 1662; I gave no year.
Culture (theatres, actresses, literature) left out because the existing entry mentions it and space was short.
